label: Government: set 3 (Sierra Leone from pre-colonial times to 1991)

papers.topic: Pre-Colonial Political Systems of the Mende and Temne
papers.title: Pre-Colonial Political Systems of the Mende and Temne: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on pre-colonial political systems of the mende and temne, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Among the pre-colonial Mende, the society that made laws, settled disputes and could check the chief was the
questions.explanation:
The Poro had political, judicial and educational roles among the Mende.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sande: The Sande (Bondo) is the women's society that trained girls.
- Ragbenle: The Ragbenle is associated with the eastern Temne.
- Freemasons: Freemasonry is a European society, not a Mende institution.

questions.stem: Kantha in Temne political tradition refers to
questions.explanation:
During kantha the chief-elect is taught the law, history and boundaries of the chiefdom.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the council of warriors that advised the chief on war: Kantha is not a council.
- the annual tribute of rice and labour paid to the chief: Tribute is not called kantha.
- the society that initiated Temne girls into womanhood: That is the Bondo society.

options.label: A
options.content: the council of warriors that advised the chief on war

options.label: B
options.content: the annual tribute of rice and labour paid to the chief

options.label: C
options.content: the society that initiated Temne girls into womanhood

options.label: D
options.content: the seclusion and instruction of a chief-elect before installation

questions.stem: A famous Mende woman ruler of the nineteenth century was
questions.explanation:
Madam Yoko ruled the Kpaa Mende from Senehun.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bai Bureh: Bai Bureh was a Temne ruler from Kasseh.
- King Naimbana: Naimbana was a Temne ruler of Koya.
- Bai Farima: Bai is a Temne title.

questions.stem: Which of the following was common to both the Mende and Temne political systems?
questions.explanation:
Both systems drew chiefs from ruling families, advised by elders and societies.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Chiefs were directly elected by all adults: Chiefs were chosen by elders and societies, not universal vote.
- All power was held by a single kingdom: Both peoples lived in many independent chiefdoms.
- Women could never hold any office: Mende women could become chiefs.

options.label: A
options.content: Chiefs were directly elected by all adults

options.label: B
options.content: All power was held by a single kingdom

options.label: C
options.content: Women could never hold any office

options.label: D
options.content: Chiefs were chosen from ruling families or houses

questions.stem: A major difference between the Temne and Mende systems was that
questions.explanation:
Muslim scholars served as advisers in many northern chiefdoms, and titles such as Alimamy were used.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Temne had no chiefs and were ruled only by elders: The Temne had paramount chiefs with titles such as Bai.
- the Mende had no secret societies of any political importance: The Mende had the Poro and Sande.
- the Mende lived only in the north and were ruled by one king: The Mende live mainly in the south and east.

options.label: A
options.content: Islam had a stronger influence on many northern Temne chiefdoms

options.label: B
options.content: the Temne had no chiefs and were ruled only by elders

options.label: C
options.content: the Mende had no secret societies of any political importance

options.label: D
options.content: the Mende lived only in the north and were ruled by one king

papers.topic: British Colonial Administration in Sierra Leone
papers.title: British Colonial Administration in Sierra Leone: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on british colonial administration in sierra leone, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Sierra Leone became a British Crown Colony in
questions.explanation:
The Colony was taken over by the Crown on 1 January 1808.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1787: 1787 was the founding of the Province of Freedom.
- 1792: 1792 was the arrival of the Nova Scotians and the founding of Freetown.
- 1896: 1896 was the declaration of the Protectorate.

questions.stem: The British declared a Protectorate over the hinterland of Sierra Leone in
questions.explanation:
The Protectorate was declared on 31 August 1896, partly to block French expansion.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1808: 1808 was when the Colony became a Crown Colony.
- 1898: 1898 was the Hut Tax War.
- 1924: 1924 was the Slater Constitution.

questions.stem: The Hut Tax of 1898 was imposed by Governor
questions.explanation:
Cardew's house tax provoked the Hut Tax War.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Alexander Ransford Slater: Slater gave his name to the 1924 Constitution.
- Hubert Stevenson: Stevenson proposed the 1951 constitution.
- Maurice Dorman: Dorman was the first Governor-General at independence.

questions.stem: The leader of resistance in the north during the Hut Tax War was
questions.explanation:
Bai Bureh of Kasseh fought a guerrilla war in 1898 before being captured and exiled.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Madam Yoko: Madam Yoko cooperated with the British.
- Siaka Stevens: Stevens was a twentieth-century politician.
- Milton Margai: Margai led Sierra Leone to independence.

questions.stem: Under indirect rule in the Protectorate, chiefs were supervised by
questions.explanation:
District Commissioners were British officers who supervised chiefs in each district.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Legislative Council: The LegCo made laws mainly for the Colony.
- the Poro society: The Poro was a traditional society, not a colonial supervisor.
- the Prime Minister: There was no Prime Minister in the colonial period.

papers.title: Colonial Constitutions of Sierra Leone: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on colonial constitutions of sierra leone, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The Executive and Legislative Councils of the Colony were created in
questions.explanation:
The 1863 Constitution set up the two councils with an official majority.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1808: 1808 was when Sierra Leone became a Crown Colony.
- 1924: 1924 introduced elected members.
- 1951: 1951 gave an African majority in the LegCo.

questions.stem: The 1924 Slater Constitution was important because it
questions.explanation:
Three members were elected by Colony voters on a limited franchise.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gave Africans a majority in the Legislative Council: That happened in 1951.
- granted full internal self-government to Sierra Leone: Independence came in 1961.
- abolished the Governor's veto over laws passed by the Council: The Governor kept the veto.

options.label: A
options.content: gave Africans a majority in the Legislative Council

options.label: B
options.content: introduced elected members into the Legislative Council for the first time

options.label: C
options.content: granted full internal self-government to Sierra Leone

options.label: D
options.content: abolished the Governor's veto over laws passed by the Council

questions.stem: Under the 1924 Constitution, the Protectorate was represented in the Legislative Council by
questions.explanation:
For the first time the Protectorate had a voice, though its representatives were nominated.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- fourteen elected members: Fourteen Protectorate members came with the 1951 constitution.
- District Commissioners only: District Commissioners were officials, not Protectorate representatives.
- members chosen by the Protectorate Assembly: The Protectorate Assembly did not exist until the 1940s.

options.label: C
options.content: three Paramount Chiefs nominated by the Governor

options.label: D
options.content: members chosen by the Protectorate Assembly

questions.stem: The constitution that first gave Africans a majority in the Legislative Council came into effect in
questions.explanation:
The 1951 (Stevenson) constitution united Colony and Protectorate members in one LegCo with an African majority.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1924: The 1924 Constitution kept an official majority.
- 1958: 1958 introduced a Premier and an all-Sierra Leonean Executive Council.
- 1961: 1961 was independence.

questions.stem: The 1951 constitution was strongly opposed by Colony leaders led by
questions.explanation:
Bankole-Bright's National Council of Sierra Leone feared Protectorate domination.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Milton Margai: Margai led the SLPP, which supported the constitution.
- Siaka Stevens: Stevens was then a member of the SLPP.
- Albert Margai: Albert Margai was an SLPP leader.

papers.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence
papers.title: Nationalism and the Road to Independence: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on nationalism and the road to independence, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The Sierra Leone branch of the West African Youth League was founded in 1938 by
questions.explanation:
Wallace-Johnson organised workers and youth and was detained in 1939.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- J. E. Casely Hayford: Casely Hayford founded the NCBWA in the Gold Coast.
- Milton Margai: Margai led the SLPP from 1951.
- Lamina Sankoh: Sankoh led the People's Party.

questions.stem: The Sierra Leone People's Party was formed in
questions.explanation:
The SLPP was formed by the merger of the SOS, the People's Party and PEPU members.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1960: 1960 was the formation of the APC.
- 1938: 1938 was the West African Youth League.
- 1946: 1946 was the Sierra Leone Organisation Society.

questions.stem: Independence for Sierra Leone was agreed at a constitutional conference held in 1960 at
questions.explanation:
The United National Front negotiated independence for 27 April 1961.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Addis Ababa: Addis Ababa hosted the founding of the OAU.
- Freetown: The conference was held in London.
- Lomé: Lomé hosted the 1999 peace agreement.

questions.stem: Siaka Stevens refused to sign the independence agreement in 1960 because he
questions.explanation:
He formed the Elections Before Independence Movement, which became the APC.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- wanted Sierra Leone to remain a British colony for ten more years: He supported independence.
- wanted to be appointed Governor-General at independence: That was not his reason.
- opposed the creation of a national Parliament for the new state: He did not oppose Parliament.

options.label: A
options.content: wanted Sierra Leone to remain a British colony for ten more years

options.label: B
options.content: wanted to be appointed Governor-General at independence

options.label: C
options.content: opposed the defence agreement and wanted elections before independence

options.label: D
options.content: opposed the creation of a national Parliament for the new state

questions.stem: Which of the following encouraged nationalism in Sierra Leone?
questions.explanation:
Soldiers returned with new ideas and expectations after fighting abroad.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The Hut Tax being abolished in 1898: The Hut Tax was not abolished in 1898.
- The absence of Western education: Western education encouraged nationalism.
- Full equality between Africans and Europeans in the civil service: Discrimination, not equality, fuelled nationalism.

options.label: A
options.content: The Hut Tax being abolished in 1898

options.label: C
options.content: Full equality between Africans and Europeans in the civil service

options.label: D
options.content: The return of ex-servicemen after the Second World War

papers.title: Independence and the 1961 Constitution: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on independence and the 1961 constitution, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Under the 1961 Constitution, the head of state of Sierra Leone was
questions.explanation:
Sierra Leone was a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth from 1961 to 1971.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Prime Minister, as leader of the majority party: The Prime Minister was head of government.
- an executive President elected by the people: An executive President came in 1971.
- the Speaker of the House of Representatives: The Speaker presided over the House.

options.label: A
options.content: the British monarch, represented by a Governor-General

options.label: B
options.content: the Prime Minister, as leader of the majority party

options.label: C
options.content: an executive President elected by the people

options.label: D
options.content: the Speaker of the House of Representatives

questions.stem: The first Prime Minister of independent Sierra Leone was
questions.explanation:
Sir Milton Margai led the SLPP government at independence.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sir Albert Margai: Albert Margai succeeded his brother in 1964.
- Siaka Stevens: Stevens became Prime Minister in 1968.
- Sir Maurice Dorman: Dorman was the first Governor-General.

questions.stem: Under the 1961 Constitution, the final court of appeal for Sierra Leone was the
questions.explanation:
Final appeals went to the Privy Council in London until 1971.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Supreme Court of Sierra Leone: The Supreme Court became final only in 1971.
- International Court of Justice: The ICJ settles disputes between states.
- ECOWAS Court of Justice: The ECOWAS Court did not then exist.

options.label: C
options.content: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

questions.stem: A weakness of the 1961 Constitution was that
questions.explanation:
Many saw a foreign head of state as incomplete independence.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it had no protection for human rights: It included fundamental rights.
- it banned opposition parties: It allowed multi-party politics.
- it had no legislature: It provided for the House of Representatives.

options.label: A
options.content: it had no protection for human rights

options.label: D
options.content: the head of state was a foreign monarch

questions.stem: The National Reformation Council ruled Sierra Leone from
questions.explanation:
The NRC, under Lt-Col Andrew Juxon-Smith, was ended by the Sergeants' revolt in 1968.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1992 to 1996: That was the NPRC.
- 1997 to 1998: That was the AFRC.
- 1971 to 1978: That was a civilian APC government.

papers.title: Republican Constitution of 1971: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on republican constitution of 1971, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The first executive President of Sierra Leone was
questions.explanation:
Stevens was sworn in as executive President on 21 April 1971.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Joseph Saidu Momoh: Momoh succeeded Stevens in 1985.
- Sir Milton Margai: Margai was Prime Minister, not President.
- Ahmad Tejan Kabbah: Kabbah was elected in 1996.

questions.stem: Under the 1971 Republican Constitution, the President was
questions.explanation:
The 1971 Constitution created an executive presidency.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a ceremonial head of state only: That describes the Governor-General under the 1961 Constitution.
- appointed by the British monarch: The republic ended the monarch's role.
- chosen by the Chief Justice: The Chief Justice does not choose the President.

options.label: A
options.content: a ceremonial head of state only

options.label: C
options.content: both head of state and head of government

questions.stem: One effect of the 1971 Constitution was that
questions.explanation:
The Supreme Court of Sierra Leone became the final court of appeal.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sierra Leone left the Commonwealth: Sierra Leone remained in the Commonwealth.
- all political parties were banned: Parties were banned only from 1978.
- the Paramount Chiefs lost their seats in Parliament: PC members remained.

options.label: C
options.content: the Paramount Chiefs lost their seats in Parliament

options.label: D
options.content: appeals to the Privy Council were abolished

questions.stem: Shortly before the republic was declared in 1971, Stevens was supported against an attempted coup by troops from
questions.explanation:
Guinea's President Sékou Touré sent troops under a defence agreement.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Nigeria: Nigerian troops came later, with ECOMOG in the 1990s.
- Britain: British troops intervened in 2000.
- Liberia: Liberia did not send troops to support Stevens.

questions.stem: A major criticism of the 1971 Constitution is that it
questions.explanation:
The powerful presidency and dominant party paved the way for the one-party state.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gave too much power to the Governor-General: The office of Governor-General was abolished.
- created a federal system: Sierra Leone remained unitary.
- made the Privy Council the final court: It ended Privy Council appeals.

options.label: A
options.content: gave too much power to the Governor-General

options.label: B
options.content: concentrated too much power in the President

options.label: D
options.content: made the Privy Council the final court

papers.title: The 1978 and 1991 Constitutions: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the 1978 and 1991 constitutions, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The 1978 Constitution made Sierra Leone
questions.explanation:
Only the APC was allowed under the 1978 Constitution.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a federal republic: Sierra Leone remained unitary.
- a constitutional monarchy: It had been a republic since 1971.
- a multi-party democracy: That was restored by the 1991 Constitution.

options.label: C
options.content: a one-party state under the APC

questions.stem: Under the 1978 Constitution, the President's term of office was
questions.explanation:
The single party candidate was elected for a seven-year term.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- five years: Five-year terms apply under the 1991 Constitution.
- four years: That is not correct for Sierra Leone.
- for life: The term was fixed at seven years.

questions.stem: The Constitutional Review Commission of 1990, which led to the 1991 Constitution, was chaired by
questions.explanation:
The Tucker Commission recommended a return to multi-party democracy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Justice Edmond Cowan: Cowan chaired the review commission of 2013–2016.
- Dr John Karefa-Smart: Karefa-Smart was a politician and party leader.
- Sir Henry Lightfoot Boston: Lightfoot Boston was Governor-General in the 1960s.

questions.stem: The 1991 Constitution of Sierra Leone came into force on
questions.explanation:
It was approved by referendum in 1991 and took effect on 1 October.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 27 April 1991: 27 April is Independence Day.
- 19 April 1991: 19 April is Republic Day.
- 29 April 1992: That was the date of the NPRC coup.

questions.stem: Under the 1991 Constitution, a President of Sierra Leone may serve
questions.explanation:
The two-term limit is an entrenched provision.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- one seven-year term only: That is not the rule in the 1991 Constitution.
- unlimited five-year terms: The 1991 Constitution sets a two-term limit.
- two seven-year terms: Terms are five years long.

options.label: C
options.content: no more than two five-year terms
